title: Decision Trees
summary: How a single decision tree splits data, where it overfits, and why it's the rare model that needs no feature scaling.

slides.markdown:
A **decision tree** learns a sequence of yes/no questions on your features — "is income > $50k?", "is age > 30?" — that carve the data into purer and purer groups until each leaf makes one prediction.

Its appeal is directness: no scaling, no linearity assumption, and you can literally print the rules and read them out loud. Its cost is that a single tree, grown freely, memorizes noise as eagerly as signal — the reason it's rarely used alone in production, but is the building block for random forests and boosting.

slides.subTitle: Recursive partitioning
slides.markdown:
A tree builds greedily, top-down: at each node, it tries every feature and every possible threshold, and picks the single split that makes the two resulting groups **purest** — most dominated by one class.

It then repeats that same search *inside* each new group, recursively, until a stopping rule kicks in (a max depth, a minimum leaf size, or no split improving purity further). The result is a tree of nested if/else rules — a path from root to leaf is one prediction rule like "income > 50k AND age > 30 → approve".

slides.subTitle: Gini vs entropy
slides.markdown:
"Purest" needs a number — an **impurity measure** scoring how mixed a group's classes are.

- **Gini impurity** — `1 − Σ p_k²`, roughly the odds of misclassifying a random item if you labeled it by the group's class proportions. Fast to compute, the default in most libraries.
- **Entropy / information gain** — `−Σ p_k log₂(p_k)`, borrowed from information theory; a split is chosen by how much it reduces entropy.

Both hit 0 for a pure group and peak for a 50/50 split; in practice they pick nearly identical splits, so the choice rarely changes results much.

Each split is a single yes/no question chosen to maximize purity gain, applied recursively down both branches.

![A decision tree growing split by split on a toy income/age dataset](assets/tree-growth.svg)

Notice the tree stops splitting a branch once a leaf is pure (or a stopping rule fires) — different branches can end up at completely different depths depending on how quickly that branch separates cleanly.

assets.alt: A decision tree growing split by split on a toy income/age dataset

slides.markdown:
Left alone, a tree keeps splitting until every leaf is pure — often a single training example per leaf. That's zero training error and terrible generalization: it has memorized noise.

Three levers rein it in: **max depth** (hard cap on how many questions deep), **min samples per leaf** (refuse a split that leaves a tiny leaf), and **pruning** (grow it fully, then cut back branches that don't improve validation accuracy). In practice, tuning max depth and min leaf size via cross-validation is the standard, cheaper alternative to full post-hoc pruning.

Trees aren't just for classification. A **regression tree** predicts a number by averaging the training targets that land in a leaf — and it picks splits to minimize **variance** within each resulting group instead of Gini or entropy.

A split is scored by how much it reduces the weighted variance of the target across the two children — the numeric analog of "purity". Everything else — recursive growth, depth limits, overfitting risk — carries over unchanged from classification trees.

Two very different ways to draw a decision surface.

| | Decision tree | Linear model |
|---|---|---|
| Boundary shape | Axis-aligned steps | Straight line/plane |
| Feature scaling | Not needed | Usually required |
| Interactions | Captured automatically | Must be hand-added |
| Extrapolation | Poor outside training range | Reasonable |

Reach for a tree when relationships are non-linear or feature interactions matter; reach for a linear model when you need smooth extrapolation or tight statistical guarantees.

**The mistake:** growing a tree to full depth and celebrating near-100% training accuracy.

**Why it breaks:** a fully-grown tree has effectively memorized each training example, including its noise and outliers — it has zero bias but enormous variance, so accuracy collapses on new data. Training accuracy alone tells you nothing about generalization here.

**The fix:** always check accuracy on a held-out validation set, and constrain depth or leaf size until the gap between train and validation accuracy closes.

slides.subTitle: Handling missing values and categorical splits natively
slides.markdown:
Most models need missing values imputed and categorical variables one-hot encoded before training — trees are the exception. Many tree implementations handle a **missing value** at split time by trying it on both branches and keeping whichever gives better validation performance, or by using a **surrogate split** (a backup feature that closely mimics the primary split's decision, used only for rows missing the primary feature).

For a **categorical feature** with a handful of values, a tree can split directly on subsets ("is region in {West, South}?") without one-hot encoding it into many binary columns first — though high-cardinality categoricals still need care, since evaluating every possible subset split becomes combinatorially expensive as the category count grows.
